title: School voucher program on student test scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Difference-in-Differences (DID) is appropriate here since we have panel data with treated and control districts observed before and after the voucher program introduction in period 4. The key assumption is parallel trends: treated and control districts would have followed similar test score trajectories in the absence of treatment. I'll test this assumption by examining pre-treatment trends.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s03_data.csv")

# Basic summary statistics
cat("Data Summary:\n")
print(summary(data))
cat("\nTreatment balance:\n")
print(table(data$treated, data$period))

# Main DID regression with unit and time fixed effects
did_model <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, data = data)
cat("\nMain DID Results:\n")
print(did_model)

# Extract and display the treatment effect
treatment_effect <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
cat("\nTreatment Effect (DID Coefficient):", round(treatment_effect, 4), "\n")

# Standard error and significance
se <- se(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
t_stat <- treatment_effect / se
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = did_model$nobs - length(coef(did_model)) - 1)
cat("Standard Error:", round(se, 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(t_stat, 4), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(p_value, 4), "\n")

# Robustness Check 1: Pre-treatment trend test
pre_treatment <- data[data$period < 4, ]
trend_test <- feols(y ~ treated * period | unit_id + period, data = pre_treatment)
cat("\nPre-treatment Trend Test (treated*period coefficient):\n")
print(summary(trend_test)$coefficients["treated:period", ])

# Robustness Check 2: Event study specification
data$rel_time <- data$period - 4
data$rel_time <- pmax(pmin(data$rel_time, 3), -3)  # Cap at +/-3 periods

# Create event study dummies (omitting period -1 as reference)
event_dummies <- paste0("i(rel_time, treated, ref = -1)")
event_study <- feols(as.formula(paste("y ~", event_dummies, "| unit_id + period")), data = data)

cat("\nEvent Study Results:\n")
print(event_study)

# Extract pre-treatment coefficients for trend test
pre_coeffs <- coef(event_study)[grepl("rel_time::-[2-3]", names(coef(event_study)))]
if(length(pre_coeffs) > 0) {
  cat("\nPre-treatment coefficients (should be close to zero):\n")
  print(round(pre_coeffs, 4))
}

# Robustness Check 3: Alternative specification without unit-specific trends
did_simple <- feols(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)
cat("\nSimple DID (without fixed effects):\n")
cat("Treatment Effect:", round(coef(did_simple)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

# Create visualization of trends
trend_data <- data %>%
  group_by(period, treated) %>%
  summarise(mean_y = mean(y), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(group = ifelse(treated == 1, "Treated", "Control"))

p <- ggplot(trend_data, aes(x = period, y = mean_y, color = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Average Test Scores by Treatment Status",
       x = "Period", y = "Average Test Score",
       color = "Group", linetype = "Group") +
  theme_minimal() +
  annotate("text", x = 4.2, y = max(trend_data$mean_y) * 0.9, 
           label = "Voucher Program\nStarts", size = 3)

print(p)

# Final summary
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULTS ===\n")
cat("DID Treatment Effect:", round(treatment_effect, 4), "\n")
cat("Statistical Significance:", ifelse(p_value < 0.05, "Significant", "Not significant"), 
    "at 5% level\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", 
    round(treatment_effect - 1.96*se, 4), ",", 
    round(treatment_effect + 1.96*se, 4), "]\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a positive treatment effect of approximately 0.1-0.3 standard deviations in test scores. School voucher programs typically show modest positive effects in the literature, particularly for disadvantaged students who gain access to higher-quality schools. The effect might be larger if the voucher program successfully enabled students to move from lower-performing public schools to higher-performing private or charter schools. However, the effect could be smaller or even null if the voucher amount was insufficient to access significantly better schools or if there were implementation challenges in the early periods after introduction.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=voucher districts, control=non-voucher; shock=program introduction
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Test scores increase significantly in voucher districts after program launch
